Who Killed Micromax?

Recommended title: Who Killed Micromax? The Indian Phone That Beat Samsung, Then Vanished

6:55Est. runtime
7Parts
50Shots
982Words

Hook

Top hooks, yt-script score

  • 44In 2014 an Indian phone brand beat Samsung in India. Five years later it had almost vanished.
  • 41A phone with a 30-day battery made Micromax India's number one. Then one SIM card killed it.

Look and device

Running device

A market-share bar chart pinned to a chai-stall wall that the story keeps cutting back to: Micromax's orange bar climbs past Nokia and Samsung, then gets eaten from the side by Jio blue and three Chinese brand colours. A crime-board 'suspects' wall in the cold open and ending ties the clues together.

Look

Punchy Indian business-history documentary in the house 2D style, Gumball/t-shirt character style (as in NVIDIA). Painted plates: a 1990s Delhi middle-class flat with a beige PC, a yellow STD/PCO booth on a dusty village road, a Gaffar Market-style phone shop, a Karva Chauth evening, a 2016 Jio launch stage, rows of Chinese brand billboards. Warm saffron and orange with Jio blue as the threat colour. SFX under the VO (ringtones, keypad beeps, crowd, cash), music only at combine.

    2014

  2. 0.02MED6.0s

  3. 0.03CU6.0s

    Five years later, it had lost almost all of its market. Who killed Micromax?

Act 1: A Boy and a 56,000-Rupee PC

0:40 · 5 shots · 95 words
  1. 1.01MED6.8s

    The story starts with Rahul Sharma, a Delhi boy from a middle-class family who studied engineering.

    A small Delhi flat; a young man with books on the bed.

    RAHUL SHARMA

    ANIMATIONCeiling fan turns; pages flip.

  2. 1.02MED10.9s

    In the 1990s he asked his father for a computer that cost about 56,000 rupees, a huge amount for a family like his. His father bought it.

    Father counting notes at a shop counter; a beige PC carried home.

    ₹56,000

    ANIMATIONNotes counted one by one; the box is lifted proudly.

  3. 1.03MED7.5s

    With no internet at home, he learned programming from books, then started writing software and supplying computer hardware.

    Rahul at the PC late at night, a C++ book open beside him.

    ANIMATIONKeyboard clatter; screen glow.

  4. 1.04MED7.9s

    In 2000, he and three friends, Vikas Jain, Rajesh Agarwal and Sumeet Kumar, set up a company called Micromax.

    Four young men around a small office desk; a hand-painted MICROMAX sign.

    MICROMAX · 2000

    ANIMATIONSign is hung; four high-fives.

  5. 1.05MED6.4s

    At first Micromax was an IT company, selling software and computer parts. Small, steady, unglamorous.

    A tiny shopfront with stacks of keyboards and CDs.

    ANIMATIONA customer counts change.

Act 2: The PCO Booth Business

1:11 · 9 shots · 171 words
  1. 2.01WIDE8.7s

    Around 2000, a mobile phone was a luxury in India. In towns and villages, people made calls from yellow STD-PCO booths.

    A yellow PCO booth on a dusty road; a queue of people waiting.

    STD · ISD · PCO

    ANIMATIONQueue shuffles; a coin drops.

  2. 2.02MED5.3s

    Those booths ran on landlines: expensive to install, messy wiring, constant repairs.

    A tangle of wires on a pole; a repairman up a ladder.

    ANIMATIONSparks; the repairman sighs.

  3. 2.03CU9.8s

    Micromax's idea: a booth phone that worked on a SIM card instead. Put in a SIM, attach an antenna, and the booth is ready.

    A chunky desk phone with an antenna and a SIM sliding in.

    SIM + ANTENNA = BOOTH

    ANIMATIONSIM clicks in; signal bars fill.

  4. 2.04MED10.9s

    They sold these wireless booth phones through telecom operators: first Airtel, then others. Every minute of every call made money for the operator, so they loved it.

    A map of India with booth icons spreading from city to city.

    ANIMATIONBooth pins pop up across India.

  5. 2.05MED10.2s

    Before that, the booth phones had one big customer: Nokia, which bought them to supply its own booth business. Revenue reached about 23 crore rupees.

    A single fat order sheet from NOKIA on the desk.

    ₹23 CRORE

    ANIMATIONOrder sheet slides in; a satisfied nod.

  6. 2.06CU9.8s

    Then, the story goes, Nokia called. It was getting out of the booth business. Micromax had a factory full of phones and no buyer.

    A phone ringing; Rahul's face falling; a warehouse of boxes behind.

    ONE BUYER. ZERO BUYERS.

    ANIMATIONRing; the receiver drops slowly.

  7. 2.07MED4.2s

    So Rahul went straight to the phone companies themselves.

    Rahul walking into a tall telecom office with a sample phone under his arm.

    ANIMATIONLift doors open.

  8. 2.08MED5.7s

    Revenue climbed past 100 crore rupees. For a while, that was the business.

    Revenue counter on the chai-stall chart ticking up.

    ₹100 CRORE+

    ANIMATIONCounter rolls.

  9. 2.09CU6.8s

    The family bought a new car. His parents finally believed this computer business might actually work.

    A shiny new car outside the flat; parents waving from the balcony.

    ANIMATIONHorn honk; balcony wave.

Act 3: The 30-Day Battery

1:04 · 8 shots · 155 words
  1. 3.01MED6.0s

    Rahul travelled through Uttar Pradesh and Bihar to see how people actually used phones.

    Rahul on a bus through farmland; villagers talking to him.

    UP · BIHAR

    ANIMATIONBus rattles; dust.

  2. 3.02CU8.3s

    He found the problem: people had phones, but the power kept going out, and batteries lasted a day or two.

    A dead phone screen; a bulb flickering off in a village house.

    ANIMATIONThe bulb dies; the phone beeps LOW BATTERY.

  3. 3.03MED9.8s

    He came back and told his team he wanted to make Micromax's own phone. They thought he was mad. Who could take on Nokia?

    Team around a table, arms crossed, one pointing at a giant NOKIA logo.

    ANIMATIONCollective groan.

  4. 3.04MED8.7s

    In 2008 they launched the Micromax X1i. Its headline feature: a battery that could last up to 30 days on standby.

    A plain candybar phone with a battery meter showing 30 DAYS.

    X1i · 30-DAY STANDBY

    ANIMATIONBattery bar fills to full and stays.

  5. 3.05CU9.4s

    Rahul got budget for a first batch of about ten thousand phones. If they didn't sell, that was the end of the idea.

    A small stack of boxes; a ticking clock above.

    10,000 PHONES

    ANIMATIONClock ticks loudly.

  6. 3.06MED5.3s

    Distributors refused to stock it. Customers only ask for Nokia, they said.

    Shop owners shaking their heads one after another.

    ANIMATIONEach shopkeeper shrugs in turn.

  7. 3.07CU8.3s

    Finally an old distributor agreed to try. The first batch, about ten thousand phones, sold out in roughly ten days.

    A shop shelf emptying in fast motion.

    SOLD OUT

    ANIMATIONBoxes vanish; till rings.

  8. 3.08CU8.7s

    The lesson Micromax took: Indian buyers wanted a phone that solved their problem, at their price, more than a famous name.

    Rahul writing on a whiteboard: PROBLEM > BRAND.

    PROBLEM > BRAND

    ANIMATIONMarker squeaks.

Act 4: Cheap, Loud and Everywhere

1:21 · 9 shots · 196 words
  1. 4.01MED10.6s

    Micromax kept spotting gaps. Most phones were designed for men. A stylish phone aimed at women, the Bling, came with sparkling crystals and a budget price.

    A glittering phone in a jewellery-style box.

    MICROMAX BLING

    ANIMATIONSparkles twinkle.

  2. 4.02MED6.4s

    At first it barely sold. Distributors said the problem was simple: nobody knew it existed.

    Full shelves gathering dust; a shopkeeper yawning.

    ANIMATIONA fly buzzes.

  3. 4.03MED9.4s

    So they ran the TV ad, with Akshay Kumar and Twinkle Khanna, right before Karva Chauth. Husbands everywhere suddenly knew what to gift.

    A TV in a living room showing the ad; a husband looking at his phone, then at his wife.

    KARVA CHAUTH

    ANIMATIONTV jingle; a lightbulb moment.

  4. 4.04MED9.1s

    Then smartphones arrived. Micromax, along with Lava and Karbonn, went after cheap Android phones. Micromax's Canvas series became the one to have.

    Three brand banners in a market; a teenager showing off a big-screen Canvas.

    CANVAS

    ANIMATIONFriends crowd around the screen.

  5. 4.05MED7.5s

    Big screens, dual SIMs and big batteries at half the price of a Samsung. Small-town India loved it.

    Spec labels around a Canvas: DUAL SIM, BIG SCREEN, BIG BATTERY, a price tag.

    ANIMATIONLabels pop on one by one.

  6. 4.06MED7.2s

    Micromax expanded into tablets, televisions and data cards, and sold phones in Russia and other markets too.

    A shop wall: phones, tablets, a TV, all orange-branded.

    ANIMATIONProducts slide onto the shelf.

  7. 4.07MED9.8s

    Most of these phones were designed with, and built by, partners in China, then branded and sold by Indian companies. That would matter later.

    Map: phones shipped from China to India with an orange sticker slapped on at the end.

    MADE IN CHINA · BRANDED IN INDIA

    ANIMATIONBoxes slide across the map; a sticker slaps on.

  8. 4.08MED13.2s

    By 2014 Micromax was on top. Research firm Counterpoint put it ahead of Samsung in Indian phone sales in one quarter. It had Hugh Jackman as its face and sponsored the Asia Cup.

    The chai-stall chart: the orange bar passes Samsung blue and Nokia.

    #1 IN INDIA · 2014

    ANIMATIONOrange bar overtakes with a whoosh.

  9. 4.09CU7.5s

    The company that once made booth phones for Nokia now sold more phones in India than Nokia did.

    A small booth phone next to a towering orange Canvas.

    ANIMATIONThe big phone grows; the little one bows.

Act 5: The Suspects

1:31 · 10 shots · 221 words
  1. 5.01MED10.9s

    Suspect number one arrived quietly: Chinese brands. Xiaomi came to India in 2014 with flash sales online. Oppo and Vivo flooded high streets with shops and billboards.

    Three new brand banners going up over the market; Micromax banners being covered.

    SUSPECT 1

    ANIMATIONBanners unroll over the orange ones.

  2. 5.02MED9.1s

    They spent heavily on ads, gave shopkeepers big margins and promoter staff in stores, and offered better cameras at the same prices.

    A shop counter where a promoter in a branded shirt talks up a Chinese phone; the shopkeeper counts a thick commission.

    ANIMATIONMoney changes hands; a selfie flash.

  3. 5.03MED13.6s

    They made their own phones and had deep pockets, close ties to chipmakers, and quick access to new parts. Micromax mostly bought designs from Chinese suppliers. Now its suppliers' own brands were its rivals.

    A Chinese factory selling the same phone to Micromax and to its own brand.

    ANIMATIONThe same phone gets two different stickers.

  4. 5.04WIDE8.3s

    Suspect number two arrived on 5 September 2016. Reliance Jio launched with free calls and free 4G data for months.

    A giant stage, blue lights, crowds; a SIM card spotlit.

    SUSPECT 2 · JIO · 5 SEP 2016

    ANIMATIONBlue lights sweep; crowd roars.

  5. 5.05MED5.3s

    Overnight, India wanted 4G phones. Micromax's warehouses were full of 3G stock.

    A warehouse stacked with 3G boxes gathering dust.

    3G STOCK

    ANIMATIONA dust cloud puffs off the boxes.

  6. 5.06MED4.9s

    Discounting that stock to clear it cost money Micromax couldn't spare.

    A shopkeeper slashing price tags with a red pen.

    SALE

    ANIMATIONPrice tags slashed.

  7. 5.07MED10.2s

    The Chinese brands already had 4G phones ready to ship. Micromax struggled to get the latest chips and modems as quickly as global brands did.

    A chip supplier handing boxes to a big brand while Micromax waits at the back of the queue.

    ANIMATIONQueue moves; Micromax's turn never comes.

  8. 5.08CU10.9s

    Suspect number three: Micromax itself. It was slow to switch, spread across tablets and TVs, and kept betting on low prices instead of building its own technology.

    A mirror on the crime-board reflecting the Micromax logo.

    SUSPECT 3?

    ANIMATIONThe mirror catches the light.

  9. 5.09MED10.6s

    The fall was fast. Micromax's share of the Indian phone market collapsed from the top spot to around one or two percent within a few years.

    The chai-stall chart: the orange bar shrinks to a sliver.

    ANIMATIONThe orange bar drains away.

  10. 5.10MED7.2s

    It wasn't alone. Lava, Karbonn, Intex and other Indian phone brands were squeezed in the same way.

    Several Indian brand banners falling down in a row like dominoes.

    ANIMATIONBanners topple one after another.

Ending: The Verdict

0:44 · 5 shots · 98 words
  1. 6.01MED10.9s

    In 2020, after the India-China border clash, Micromax tried a comeback with a new 'In' brand pitched as Indian. It got headlines, but not the market back.

    A new phone launch with 'IN' on stage; a small cheering crowd.

    MICROMAX IN · 2020

    ANIMATIONSpotlights; polite applause.

  2. 6.02MED9.1s

    The founders moved on. The companies around them, including electronics manufacturing businesses, kept going, but the Micromax that beat Samsung was gone.

    The four founders walking out of a factory gate in different directions.

    ANIMATIONGate closes behind them.

  3. 6.03CU10.9s

    So who killed Micromax? Jio pulled the trigger, Chinese rivals were already waiting, and a business built on other people's technology had nothing to fight back with.

    The crime-board: string connects all three suspects at once.

    VERDICT

    ANIMATIONString pulls tight between all three.

  4. 6.04CU9.1s

    It's a lesson for every Indian start-up: being cheap gets you in the door. Owning the technology keeps you in the room.

    A young founder at a desk with a chip in their hand.

    ANIMATIONPush in on the chip.

  5. 6.05TITLE4.0s

    (no narration)

    End card.

    WHO KILLED MICROMAX?

    ANIMATIONRingtone fades out.

Fact log

Fixes against the transcript

  • Co-founders: Rahul Sharma, Vikas Jain, Rajesh Agarwal, Sumeet Kumar (Micromax Informatics, 2000).
  • First Micromax handset X1i launched 2008 with up to 30 days standby battery (standby, not talk time).
  • Q2 2014: Micromax #1 in India smartphone shipments per Canalys (Counterpoint had it #1 in overall phones in a 2014 quarter). Script says one research firm, one quarter; CHECK which firm before VO and keep it to one.
  • Hugh Jackman ambassador 2013; Asia Cup sponsorship 2014.
  • Jio commercial launch 5 Sept 2016 (Welcome Offer: free voice and data to March 2017).
  • Xiaomi India entry July 2014; Oppo and Vivo expanded offline 2015-2017 (transcript's 'overnight with Jio' corrected).
  • Market share by 2018-19 around 1-2% (Counterpoint/IDC); transcript's '90% of business lost' replaced with share figures.
  • Micromax 'In' sub-brand launched November 2020 after June 2020 Galwan clash.
  • Transcript valuation ($3.5B) and '12,000 crore company' dropped as unverified.
  • 'Bling' phone with Swarovski elements; ad with Akshay Kumar and Twinkle Khanna per transcript; Karva Chauth timing per transcript (anecdote).

Removed from the transcript

  • Interview clips and English news soundbites replaced with narration.
  • Unverified valuation and revenue figures dropped.
